# HNSecW: A Logarithmic-Time MPC Protocol for Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search ### ABSTRACT As a core component of modern RAG systems, approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search has been extensively studied for decades. In practice, deploying ANN often requires symmetric privacy, where the querier’s query and the database owner’s data must remain hidden from each other, necessitating a secure multi-party computation (MPC) solution. So far, most MPC-based ANN protocols follow a cluster-based approach: they evaluate distances for the query over a large candidate set and rely on heavyweight primitives such as distributed ORAM to hide access patterns. As a result, each search typically requires \(O(\sqrt{N})\) time. We propose HNSecW, a novel MPC protocol for ANN search that achieves the _O_(log_N_) search time for the first time. We first study the _single-query_ setting. Starting from HNSW, the state-of-the-art ANN algorithm, we redesign its control flow and data structures to achieve fully data-independent execution. To further achieve logarithmic search time, we employ offline reshuffling and partial database duplication. Furthermore, we extend our protocol to support _multiple sequential queries_ by introducing a "double visited" caching structure that eliminates redundant cross-query memory accesses, thereby avoiding per-query online shuffling. In addition, we develop a _batch-query_ protocol that exploits higher parallelism to reduce both round complexity and the circuit’s critical path. Our experiments show that HNSecW preserves the high accuracy of plaintext HNSW (\(\ge\) 90% recall) and delivers over a 20\(\times\) efficiency improvement over prior work on million-scale datasets. **PVLDB Reference Format:** Fahong Zhang, Weijie Jin, Lixu Wang, Ning Luo, Xiao Wang, and Wei Dong. So far, designing an efficient ANN algorithm for a large-sized high- dimensional database has been well studied for decades [29, 30, 43]. However, in real-world ANN applications, security and privacy concerns arise [6, 31, 48]. Without a protective protocol, either the querier submits the query in plaintext to the database owner, who executes the ANN algorithm, or the computation is delegated to the querier, which typically requires the database owner to reveal (at least part of) its data to enable search. The former violates query privacy, whereas the latter compromises database privacy. This motivates a symmetric private ANN model that simultaneously protects both the query and the database. We illustrate the need for symmetric privacy through two representative scenarios: _Example 1.1. In a joint healthcare study, a research institute (querier) prepares a drug trial by querying a hospital’s (database owner) private gene-expression database for similar patient profiles. The hospital returns only the top records allowed by the data-use agreement, and the institute uses them as LLM context to generate a trial plan. During the collaboration, disclosing the query may reveal the institute’s research details; disclosing the hospital’s database and patient data would violate regulations such as HIPAA._ _Example 1.2. During a cyber incident, a security team (querier) queries a vendor’s (database owner) private threat intelligence database for the closest matching attack reports and indicators, and uses the results to identify the threat and respond promptly. Disclosing the query can reveal what systems were hit; if the database is disclosed, it can expose sensitive intelligence sources and customer incidents._ A naive approach to achieving symmetric privacy is to introduce a trusted third party, such as a cloud provider: both the database owner and the querier submit their plaintext vector database and queries to the third party, which then performs the ANN search ∗Corresponding author. This motivates people to seek cryptographic solutions that can remove the need for trusted third parties. One natural solution is to implement ANN search in the secure multi-party computation (MPC) model \[47\]. In these solutions, the database owner and the querier secret-share the vector database and queries across multiple servers. The servers then jointly execute the ANN search protocol on these shares. The security of MPC ensures that no single server can reconstruct any input. Several recent efforts pursue this direction. However, most existing solutions either relax privacy guarantees by assuming a public database \[50\], or incur high computational overhead \[11, 28\]. Specifically, the two closest MPC solutions to our setting \[11, 28\] rely on cluster-based ANN pipelines: the database of size _N_ is partitioned into clusters, and the protocol identifies and searches the clusters most relevant to a query. Their efficiency depends heavily on the number of clusters, which is typically set to \(\sqrt{N}\) to balance cluster selection and in-cluster search costs. As a result, their search time becomes \(O(\sqrt{N})\) for each query. This quickly becomes impractical at modern database scales, because under MPC, each additional vector access incurs heavy communication, particularly for high-dimensional vectors. Earlier secure _k_NN works \[34, 36, 38, 53\] target smaller-scale or specialized two-party settings rather than scalable secret-shared ANN.

This motivates us to develop a more efficient MPC ANN protocol. The natural idea is to deploy a state-of-the-art hierarchical graph-based ANN algorithm, such as HNSW \[32\], under the MPC setting. By building a multi-layer graph index over the database, such algorithms enable efficient search: the query starts at the top layer, takes only a few steps per layer, and then moves to lower layers. It is widely accepted that, in practice, these indexes visit only _O_(log_N_) out of _N_ vectors per query in expectation, where _N_ is the database size.

However, implementing this hierarchical graph-based search in MPC is very challenging. At a high level, we must make two parts of the algorithm oblivious: (i) the search logic, e.g., when to stop the search, and (ii) the access pattern. The stopping condition in HNSW is highly data- and query-dependent and replacing it with data-independent predicates without careful consideration totally compromises efficiency. For the access pattern, the search process may revisit the same node or vector multiple times, creating highly non-uniform and query-dependent memory accesses. Some naive approaches to hide such redundant access patterns, such as ORAM \[18\], would incur prohibitive communication overhead. Therefore, this naturally raises a fundamental research question:

### 1.1 Our Results

In this paper, we give a positive answer to the above question by proposing the first MPC ANN protocol with logarithmic online query complexity. Our protocol starts from the SOTA hierarchical graph index HNSW. We first study the single-query setting. To make the search logic fully oblivious, we design a data-independent control flow with a fixed search-termination bound and redesign all data structures as fixed-size arrays that support oblivious updates.

To achieve an oblivious access pattern, we combine offline random reshuffling with a duplicated vector database, yielding _O_(1) online overhead for each graph-index and vector access. Overall, our single-query MPC protocol achieves logarithmic online search complexity with at most a \(2\times\) increase in vector storage. Moreover, we extend this design to support multiple queries. To handle repeated accesses across queries while avoiding additional online reshuffling, we introduce cross-query "double visited" structures that cache the graph nodes and vectors accessed by earlier queries, enabling later queries to reuse the cached information without revisiting the graph index and vector database. In summary, our results are as follows:

(1) **Single query.** For a single query, HNSecW achieves _O_(log_N_) online searching complexity over a database of size _N_. As  1 shows, HNSecW substantially outperforms state-of-the-art secure ANN baselines (SANNS \[11\], PANTHER \[28\]), whose clustering- based pipelines have online communication that scales as \(\sqrt{N}\).

(2) **Multiple queries.** For _U_ sequential queries, we propose a multi-query protocol with an amortized cost of _O(U_log_N_). Unlike schemes requiring reshuffling per query (e.g., PANTHER \[28\]), our protocol allows _U_ queries to share a single offline reshuffle, avoiding additional online overhead.

(3) **Parallelism and batch queries.** Additionally, we design parallel implementations of the above protocols: for the single-query protocol, the critical-path length is _O_(log_N_), and for the multiple- query protocol, it is _O(U_log_N_). We also propose a batch-query protocol with higher parallelism that processes a batch of _U_ queries simultaneously with a much lower critical-path length of _O_(log<sup>2</sup>_U_+log_N_).

(4) **Empirical evaluation.** We conduct a comprehensive experiment on large-scale ANN benchmarks. HNSecW reaches recall over 0.9, matching the state-of-the-art plaintext ANN algorithm. At the same target recall, HNSecW achieves up to \(22\times\) WAN speedup and \(46\times\) less communication versus 2PC PANTHER; against the exact- top-_k_ 3PC SORT baseline, it achieves up to \(1.6k\times\) WAN speedup and \(617\times\) less communication. All code is now available <sup>1</sup>.

return W ## 2.1 Notation Let \(\mathcal{D}=\{\vec{v}_0,\vec{v}_1,\dots,\vec{v}_{N-1}\}\) be a dataset of _N_ vectors in R_d_, where _d_ is the dimension. We use \(\vec{v}[j]\) to denote the _j_-th coordinate of vector \(\vec{v}\). Let \(dist:\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}^d\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) denote a vector distance function. The index set is \[_N_\]:={0,1_,...,N_-1}. For any set S, |S| is its cardinality. A graph G=(V,E) has vertices \(\mathcal{V}\subseteq\mathcal{D}\) and undirected edges E. For any \(\vec{v}\in\mathcal{V}\), \(\mathcal{N}(\vec{v})\) denotes its neighbor set. ## 2.2 _k_-Nearest Neighbor Search For the _k_-nearest neighbor (_k_-NN) problem, we have a dataset D of _N_ vectors in R_d_ and a query vector \(\vec{q}\in\mathbb{R}^d\). The goal is to find the subset \(\mathcal{D}_k^*(\vec{q})\subseteq\mathcal{D}\) such that \(|\mathcal{D}_k^*(\vec{q})|=k\), and for any \(\vec{v}\in\mathcal{D}_k^*(\vec{q})\) and any \(\vec{v}'\in\mathcal{D}\backslash\mathcal{D}_k^*(\vec{q})\), it holds that \(dist(\vec{v},\vec{q})\le dist(\vec{v}',\vec{q})\). A straightforward approach is the linear scan, which computes the distance from \(\vec{q}\) to all _N_ vectors and maintains the _k_ smallest distances found so far, typically using a priority queue of size _k_. The computational cost is _O(Nd+Nlogk_), prohibitive for large-scale datasets (large _N_) or high-dimensional data (large _d_). To address the _O(Nd+Nlogk_) cost, graph-based _k_-NN approaches have been proposed. These methods operate on a graph G=(D,E) over the dataset D, where each vector in R_d_ is represented as a vertex, and edges connect pairs of sufficiently "close" vectors. Given a query \(\vec{q}\), the search greedily traverses the graph from an initial node toward nodes closer to \(\vec{q}\). A representative example is the Delaunay graph \[13\]. In the two-dimensional case, each node in the Delaunay graph has an expected degree of _O_(1), and it guarantees that for any query \(\vec{q}\), the exact nearest neighbor can be found in expected _O_(log_N_) time \[32\]. However, moving towards the general case, the average node degree in the Delaunay graph grows exponentially in vector dimension with \(O(N^{\lceil d/2\rceil})\) \[13\], making search impractical. ## 2.3 Approximate _k_-NN and Hierarchical Navigable Small World Given that existing _k_-NN search algorithms are infeasible for large- scale, high-dimensional data, where both linear scan and ideal graph-based methods are prohibitively expensive, a practical trade- off between accuracy and efficiency is necessary. Consequently, people have proposed the _Approximate k-NN (ANN)_. In ANN, instead of returning the exact nearest set \(\mathcal{D}_k^*(\vec{q})\), the goal is to find an approximate set S that meets a target Recall \(R\in(0,1]\), defined as \(\text{Recall}(\mathcal{S})=|\mathcal{S}\cap\mathcal{D}_k^*(\vec{q})|/k\ge R\). Over the years, various families of ANN methods have been developed, including hashing-based, tree- based, and quantization-based approaches. Among them, Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) \[32\], achieves state-of-the-art query performance for high-dimensional data \[32\]. The core of HNSW is a multi-layered graph structure G={G0,G1_,...,_G_L_-1}, where each layer \(\mathcal{G}_\ell=(\mathcal{V}_\ell,\mathcal{E}_\ell)\) denotes a graph whose nodes correspond to vectors in the dataset D. The layers form a sequence of nested subsets of D: \(\mathcal{V}_{L-1}\subset\mathcal{V}_{L-2}\subset\cdots\subset\mathcal{V}_1\subset\mathcal{V}_0=\mathcal{D}\). The number of nodes decreases geometrically from bottom to top, resulting in _L=O_(log_N_) layers. The edges are constructed from the nodes’ underlying vector representations, and each \(\mathcal{G}_\ell\) serves as an out-degree bound _M=O_(1) approximation of a Delaunay graph. This hierarchical graph G is an efficient index for the vector database D. Its design enables a two-phase search strategy: upper, sparser layers support coarse-grained navigation, ensuring high search efficiency, while lower, denser layers provide fine-grained refinement, ensuring high search accuracy. For query \(\vec{q}\in\mathbb{R}^d\), HNSW starts at a random entry point in the top layer G_L_-1. Each layer search locates the locally closest node to \(\vec{q}\), which becomes the entry point for the next lower layer. After searching the base layer G0, the algorithm returns the _k_ nearest neighbors of \(\vec{q}\) from all visited nodes. To implement this idea, at each layer the search maintains three data structures: a candidate set _C_, which stores potential nodes for further exploration; a result set _W_, which stores the closest nodes found so far, where |_W_|=_ef_ with _ef_=1 for non-base layers and _ef=O(k_) for the base layer; and a visited set _V_ , which records all visited nodes to prevent revisits. All these data structures are initialized with the entry point _ep_, and the search then proceeds iteratively. At each iteration, we extract the nearest candidate _c_ from _C_, explore each unvisited neighbor _e_ of _c_, and add them to _V_ . If _e_ is closer to \(\vec{q}\) than the farthest node in _W_, it is inserted into both _C_ and _W_, and _W_ is kept at size at most _ef_. The search terminates when no candidate in _C_ is closer to \(\vec{q}\) than the farthest node in _W_, or when _C_ becomes empty. Algorithm 1 gives the detailed procedure. We abstract HNSW into three key components: the **search logic flow**, the **data structures**, and the **graph and vector access**. The logic flow specifies how the search proceeds within each layer. In each step, it moves to the nearest candidate node and then explores all its neighbors. The search stops when no candidate is closer to the query than the current results. The data structures support this process. At each layer, the algorithm maintains three sets: a candidate set _C_, a result set _W_, and a visited set _V_ . Finally, the logic flow interacts with the underlying graph index and vector database. For each candidate _c_, the search first accesses the graph index to

retrieve its neighbor list, then accesses the vector database to obtain these neighbors’ vectors for distance computation.

### 2.4 Secure Multi-Party Computation

Secure multi-party computation (MPC) enables multiple parties to jointly compute a function over their private inputs while only revealing the output to designated parties [47]. We use secret-sharing MPC protocols where, for each intermediate value _x_, all parties hold its secret sharing denoted as \(\unknown x\unknown\). The security ensures that the adversary cannot learn the value even when corrupting some number of parties as allowed by the threat model. Our system treats MPC protocols as black boxes; thus, we describe computation directly over secret shares. In particular, we use \(\unknown x\unknown+\unknown y\unknown\) and \(\unknown x\unknown\times\unknown y\unknown\) to denote addition and multiplication in MPC over secret-shared values. Typically, given network bandwidth BW and round-trip time RTT, MPC protocols follow this online latency model:

\(T_\text{online}\approx\text{Round}\cdot\text{RTT}+\frac{\text{Communication}}{\text{BW}}+\text{Computation}.\)

Here, Computation is each party’s local, non-interactive work and is often almost free. Communication is the total data exchanged and scales linearly with the multiplication gate count. Round is the number of sequential interaction steps, determined by the circuit’s multiplicative depth.

**Making Algorithms Oblivious.** Under MPC, oblivious execution has three requirements:

(1) **Logic flow.** For fixed public parameters, the algorithm follows the same sequence of operations. For example, each loop runs for a fixed number of iterations.

(2) **Data structures.** For fixed public parameters, intermediate data structures have the same sizes and update schedule.

(3) **Data access pattern.** For fixed public parameters, physical- address sequences are indistinguishable across private inputs.

**Oblivious Access in MPC.** Among these requirements, oblivious data access has been widely studied as a general primitive. MPC protocols based on secret-sharing can typically support any circuit, but random accesses are expensive to represent as circuits. To support private accesses on large arrays without incurring a cost linear to the array, one would need to use an Oblivious RAM (ORAM) [18] by executing the ORAM client in MPC [19]. This protocol is also called Distributed ORAM (DORAM). Given a secret-shared array \(\unknown\vec{v}\unknown\) and secret-shared index \(\unknown i\unknown\), DORAM enables parties to jointly compute \(\unknown\vec{v}[\unknown i\unknown]\unknown\) (the secret-shared value at secret-shared position) without revealing the index or the value to any party. DORAM has been optimized in different ways, including circuit-based minimization (e.g., [44]) and protocol-level adaptation (e.g., [14]). Although the most efficient construction can achieve _O_(log_N_) communication overhead [39], DORAM still incurs an _O(N_) computational cost. Moreover, DORAM accesses are stateful and often sequential, making batched accesses difficult to parallelize. Therefore, rather than directly adopting generic DORAM in our MPC protocol, we propose a specialized algorithm to implement an oblivious access pattern.

**Security Models.** Beyond these requirements, oblivious algorithm design also depends on the security model. For secure ANN, we distinguish four models based on who has plaintext access to each input and who performs the search, from general to specific:

(1) **Symmetric MPC.** The computation parties have no access to the database, index, or query in plaintext. They perform the search over secret values. This is also the standard setting in the MPC literature. Our paper targets this model for data collaboration between untrusted organizations and computation outsourcing by a single data owner.

(2) **Client-server search.** The client has plaintext access to the query, while the server has plaintext access to the database and index. They jointly perform the search without learning the other’s input beyond the result. SANNS and PANTHER follow this model [11, 28].

(3) **Storage outsourcing.** The client has plaintext access to the database, index, and query. It encrypts the database and index and then outsources them to an untrusted server. During search, the client retrieves data from the server and performs the search locally. Compass follows this model [51].

(4) **Query-private search.** The client has plaintext access to the query. The database and index are public and stored on the server, so both the client and server have plaintext access to them. During search, the client retrieves database and index entries from the server and searches locally. Thus, only the query is hidden from the server. Pacmann follows this model [50].

We consider a private HNSW search involving two input-holding parties and a set of _s_ MPC servers; Figure 1 gives the high-level architecture. ## 3.2 Single-Query

Even when all vectors and their distance to the query are kept secret, a single HNSW query is not oblivious in its control flow, data structures, or graph and vector access patterns, all depending on the underlying graph and query. Achieving obliviousness to prevent leakage requires a dedicated analysis of the performance features that HNSW presents, since a generic method that follows only worst-case conditions would introduce prohibitive overhead. In our protocol, we design customized optimizations to make each part oblivious by taking advantage of its unique features. For a single query, we traverse each layer without revealing the access pattern. At every layer, we use our oblivious data structure to maintain the search state, and we terminate the traversal using a tailored termination condition that prevents information leakage. We outline the key ideas here, with full details in Section 4.

\(\bullet\) **Control flow.** We eliminate data-dependent stopping conditions by replacing them with a fixed iteration bound derived from a detailed analysis of HNSW’s stopping behavior, ensuring obliviousness with only negligible recall loss (Section 4.1). Although there is no theoretical bound on the iterations, we found that in the specific context of RAG, we could set a tight upper bound on the number of iterations without degrading the end-to-end performance.

\(\bullet\) **Data structure.** We observe that both the candidate set and the result set exhibit a monotonic exclusion property: once a node is excluded, it will not be included in these sets again. Using this monotonicity, we design an oblivious data structure for both sets that keeps them at a fixed size and removes farther nodes through fixed-size tail truncation after oblivious sorting (Section 4.2).

\(\bullet\) **Graph and vector access pattern.** We use the fact that HNSW naturally avoids revisiting a node more than once per layer. To further reduce redundant access across the layers, we assign each layer an independently shuffled graph and vector tables so every address is accessed at most once, yielding fully oblivious access patterns.

## 3.3 Multiple-Query

Extending the single-query protocol to multiple queries introduces a fundamentally new challenge: different queries may revisit the same graph node and its associated vector. Hiding these repeated visits would require reshuffling the graph and vector tables after every query. However, such per-query reshuffling is impractical in an online setting due to the significant latency it entails. To address this, we rely on the insight that once data has been accessed, it can be cached and reused across queries rather than accessed repeatedly. We propose to use two global cross-query visited structures, one for graph neighbor lists and one for vector contents. These structures serve as a secure shared cache: once any query retrieves a node or vector, it is stored in the global visited array. Subsequent queries check this array first and reuse the cached data. As a result, each graph or vector access first scans the cache and then performs a real or dummy data-access step. Under this design, every node and vector is accessed at most once from the underlying shuffled tables globally, while subsequent revisits are served through oblivious cache scans. Combined with one-time random pre-shuffling, this keeps the overall access pattern oblivious; see Section 5.

## 3.4 Parallel-Enhanced Batch Model

Furthermore, we consider how the oblivious HNSW search can be executed in parallel. The single-query protocol already exhibits high parallelism, but its multiple-query extension is designed to process the _U_ queries sequentially, giving a linear circuit depth of _O(U_). In a batch setting where many queries are available simultaneously, it is natural to ask whether the computation can be reorganized to reduce this depth to better exploit parallel execution. As in the multiple-query setting, the fundamental challenge is to avoid accesses to the same nodes and vectors across queries. A naive approach is to cache every accessed element (neighbor lists and vectors), as in the sequential protocol. But in the batch setting, such a large cache is unnecessary. Our key insight is that, because all queries proceed in synchronized iterations, we do not passively wait for cache hits and reuse; instead, we force \(U\cdot M\) accessed vectors to be evaluated against _U_ queries: if a query later needs that vector, it can skip the inner path; if not, the extra evaluation does not affect correctness. This eliminates the need for a massive cache and naturally prevents redundant accesses. As a result, the batch-query protocol achieves a depth of _O_(log<sup>2</sup>_U_+log_N_), coming from the oblivious duplicate removal of the \(U\cdot M\) neighbors per iteration plus the _O_(log_N_) HNSW layers.

## 4 SINGLE QUERY PROOL

As discussed in Section 2, we decompose HNSW search into three components: the search logic flow, the data structures, and the graph/vector access patterns. In this section, we briefly outline how to make each component oblivious. Section 4.1 makes the control flow data-independent by replacing the original data-dependent stopping conditions with a fixed iteration bound. Section 4.2 redesigns the visited, candidate, and result structures as fixed-size arrays with uniform update rules. Section 4.3 ensures oblivious graph and vector access by avoiding repeated retrievals through per-layer reshuffled tables. Finally, Section 4.4 assembles these building blocks into the complete oblivious single-query protocol.

### 4.1 Making Logic Flow Oblivious

We first make HNSW’s search logic flow oblivious. At each layer, original HNSW iteratively finds the nearest candidate node and explores all its neighbors. The logic flow is inherently data-dependent.

The first source of data dependence is varying node degrees: exposing this variation would leak information about the graph and query. Fortunately, this dependency is easy to remove. Since HNSW enforces an out-degree upper bound _M_ per node, we pad each node’s neighbor list with randomly selected nodes from the same layer to obtain a fixed length of _M_. This padding does not reduce search quality: all real neighbors remain available for selection.

The more subtle challenge lies in the termination condition. In HNSW, the search stops when no better candidate remains (line 7-8 in Algorithm 1), or when the candidate set becomes empty (line 4 in Algorithm 1). Both conditions are inherently data-dependent. At first glance, this seems similar to the bounded-degree case, since the original HNSW paper \[32\] suggests that each layer can be traversed in a constant number of hops. One may use that constant as a fixed upper bound and pad execution with dummy searches. However, unlike node degree, this constant is not a worst-case bound; it arises from an expected-case analysis in \[32\] that assumes each layer forms a perfect Delaunay graph \[13\]. Real HNSW layers only approximate such structures, so the constant-hop guarantee does not hold in general. In fact, the best-known asymptotic bound for HNSW on arbitrary data is still _O(N_). A practical, data-independent iteration bound must therefore be derived from the actual termination behavior.

The first termination condition (lines 7-8 in Algorithm 1) triggers when the closest candidate can no longer improve the current result set. This can only happen after _ef_ search steps. Since every<tbc>

<tbc>node inserted into _W_ is also inserted into _C_, every node in the final _W_ must have been popped from _C_ and explored (i.e., cannot remain in _C_); otherwise, it would stay in _C_ and lead to \(min(C)\le max(W)\), contradicting the stopping condition. Hence, letting _s_ denote the number of search steps performed by standard HNSW at a given layer, we always have \(s\ge ef\) and can write exact search steps as \(s=ef+\Delta\), where residual \(\Delta\) captures work beyond the _ef_ steps. Therefore, to make the termination condition oblivious, a natural approach is to fix the number of search steps at each layer. Specifically, for each layer \(\ell\), we set the number of search steps to \(T^{(\ell)}=ef^{(\ell)}+\overline{\Delta^{(\ell)}}\), where \(\overline{\Delta^{(\ell)}}\) is a public upper parameter to bound the residual term and depends only on public quantities such as _N_, _d_, and _M_. Below, we present our strategy for setting \(ef^{(\ell)}\) and \(\overline{\Delta^{(\ell)}}\), both bounded by logarithmic terms, and show the resulting procedure performs robustly in practice. _However, designing termination strategies for HNSW that balance accuracy and efficiency remains an active research topic even in the non-private setting \[8\], and is not the main interest of this paper. Future termination strategies can also be integrated into our framework. Moreover, we highlight that, as long as the number of search steps increases by at most a logarithmic factor, our final complexity guarantee remains unchanged._

## 4.2 Making Data Structures Oblivious

We next make the data structures of HNSW oblivious. Recall that each layer individually maintains three structures: the visited set _V_ , the candidate set _C_, and the result set _W_. However, the sizes and update frequencies of the three sets are inherently data- and query-dependent during search. We therefore redesign them into oblivious counterparts.

### 4.2.1 Oblivious Result Set W.

The result set _W_ is easier to make oblivious than _C_ and _V_ because original HNSW already bounds its size by _ef_. The only data-dependent behavior is the conditional insertion rule, i.e., inserting a node into _W_ when it improves the current _ef_ results and passes the visited check (line 13 in Algorithm 1). We remove this data-dependent condition by obliviously considering every node for insertion, at a cost of _O(ef_) per node.<sup>2</sup> Overall, this naive approach costs \(O(M\cdot ef)\) in each iteration. For practical efficiency, we instead insert all _M_ elements, apply oblivious sorting, and then reduce the size back to _ef_, incurring only _O(ef_log<sup>2</sup>(_ef_)) complexity. Since log<sup>2</sup>(_ef_) is much smaller than _M_ in our setting, this approach outperforms the naive alternative in practice.

### 4.2.2 Oblivious Visited Set V.

The visited set _V_ records explored nodes to prevent later revisits. In the original HNSW, _V_ is a dynamic set whose size and insertion pattern are both query- and data- dependent, since nodes are inserted only when first encountered and their growth is unpredictable. To eliminate this dependence, we observe that _V_ can safely contain duplicate nodes. We therefore replace the set, whose size is unpredictable, with a list whose size increases by exactly one after each exploration. More precisely, each iteration appends all _M_ neighbors, regardless of whether they have appeared before, so that _V_ contains exactly \(M\cdot T+1\) entries after _T_ iterations. A full linear scan of this list performs a visited check at a cost of _O(MT_), which is scalable and independent of _N_.

### 4.2.3 Oblivious Candidate Set C.

The candidate set _C_ stores the nodes awaiting expansion and is also a fully dynamic set. In the original HNSW, its size is inherently data-dependent: each iteration extracts one node from the set but may insert zero, a few, or up to _M_ new nodes. The insertion condition is also data-dependent, since neighbors are added to _C_ only when they pass the visited check and could improve the result set _W_ (line 10, 13 in Algorithm 1). To make _C_ oblivious, we leverage the fixed iteration _T_ established in Section 4.1. Since at most _T_ candidates will be extracted, entries beyond the top-_T_ positions cannot be used and need not be retained. We therefore replace the dynamic set with a fixed-length array of size _T_. In every iteration, all _M_ neighbors, whether real or dummy after the visited check, are appended to _C_. We then perform an oblivious sort by distance and retain only the top-_T_ entries. As we discussed earlier, since dummy nodes carry a maximum distance _d_max, they always expand to other dummy nodes. They cannot influence the result set _W_ even if they are selected after the real nodes are exhausted in _C_. This fixed-size and fixed-update design of _C_ eliminates data-dependent behavior while preserving original HNSW’s functionality.

## 4.3 Making Access Patterns Oblivious

The HNSW search process involves two types of data access: vector access and graph access. During the search, a node first incurs a vector access where its distance to the query is evaluated. If the node is later selected for expansion (extracted from the candidate list _C_), it then incurs a graph access to retrieve its neighbor list. A straightforward way to make both accesses oblivious is to store the graphs and the vector database in DORAM. However, this incurs significant overhead, as each access requires \(O(logN_\ell)\) time.

To design a more efficient solution, we recall that achieving oblivious access requires two properties: data anonymization, which can be easily achieved through pre-shuffling, and non-repetitive access, where no address is revisited within a query. In this single- query setting, we assume that both graph and vector data have been anonymized through offline reshuffling. Therefore, if each item is retrieved at most once, the access is oblivious. We now analyze where repeated accesses arise and how to avoid them.

Within a single layer, both graph and vector accesses are non- repetitive. The visited set prevents revisiting any node, so its neighbor list and its vector are retrieved at most once. Across layers, the search may revisit a logical node because each layer builds a separate, increasingly refined neighborhood structure, and the same node provides different information at each layer. ### 4.4 Put It All Together

We now integrate the oblivious control flow, data structures, and access patterns into a complete single query HNSW protocol under MPC. Here, we first describe how the per-layer data is represented and secret-shared. At each layer \(\ell\), the data owner provides two tables: a graph table \(\mathcal{G}_\ell\) containing neighbor lists as the HNSW index and a vector table \(\mathcal{D}_\ell\) containing the node vectors. Both tables are padded with _TM+T+ef_ dummies, where _TM_ is for visited check, while _T+ef_ is for initialization of _C_ and _W_. After padding, MPC parties secret-share and jointly reshuffle the tables offline. Each graph table entry stores _M_ neighbors’ vector-table addresses, \(\mathcal{G}_\ell[i]=(\unknown n_{i,0}\unknown,\dots,\unknown n_{i,M-1}\unknown)\), where \(\mathcal{D}_\ell[n_{i,j}]\) would return the _j_-th neighbor’s vector and auxiliary information. Each vector table entry is \(\mathcal{D}_\ell[j]=(\unknown\vec{v}_j\unknown,\unknown a_j\unknown,\unknown b_j\unknown,\unknown m_j\unknown)\), where \(\vec{v}_j\) is the node’s vector; _a<sub>j</sub>_ is the graph table address of the nodes; _b<sub>j</sub>_ is the address of the same vector in \(\mathcal{D}_{\ell-1}\) (used during layer transition); and \(m_j\in\{0,1\}\) is the dummy entry flag. We collect all dummy vector addresses in a pool \(\text{DUM}_\ell=(\unknown d_0\unknown,\dots,\unknown d_{MT+T+ef-1}\unknown)\).

During the search, MPC parties jointly maintain three fixed- size arrays at each layer: \(V=\{\unknown a_i\unknown\}_{i=0}^{MT}\), \(C=((\unknown c_i\unknown,\unknown d_i\unknown))_{i=0}^{T-1}\), and \(W=((\unknown w_i\unknown,\unknown b_i\unknown,\unknown\delta_i\unknown))_{i=0}^{ef-1}\). Here _V_ stores the vector-table addresses _a<sub>i</sub>_ of visited nodes; _C_ stores the graph-table addresses _c<sub>i</sub>_ and distances _d<sub>i</sub>_ of candidate nodes; _W_ stores the vector-table address _w<sub>i</sub>_, the lower-layer vector address _b<sub>i</sub>_, and the distance \(\delta_i\) of the current top-_ef_ results nodes.

With the oblivious data structures in place, Algorithm 2 specifies the per-layer search, which runs a fixed number of iterations and updates _V_ , _C_, and _W_ obliviously. The full single-query protocol (Algorithm 3) applies this layer search from the top layer to the base. At the base layer, _W_<sub>0</sub> stores only vector-table addresses for efficient oblivious sorting; the actual vectors are fetched from an auxiliary reshuffled table D<sub>-1</sub>. Since the base layer may place dummy addresses among the top-_k_ when _k_ is large, D<sub>-1</sub> is padded with _MT+T+ef_ dummy entries containing application-safe vectors so that dummy outputs remain indistinguishable from real ones.

## 5.1 Double Visitor Arrays

The challenge in the multiple-query setting is that later queries may need to access nodes and vectors that earlier queries already accessed. As noted above, the single-query protocol prevents repeated data access with an array _V_ tracking previously accessed nodes. Moving to the multiple-query setting, one straightforward idea is to simply make _V_ global, so that each node can be accessed by only one query. However, queries may have overlapping search<tbc>

<tbc>paths, so simply globalizing _V_ would make multi-query HNSW search incorrect.

To address this issue, we propose two global cross-query caches recording all nodes and vectors accessed so far. Specifically, we maintain a graph-side visited set \(V_\ell^\mathcal{G}\) and a vector-side visited set \(V_\ell^\mathcal{D}\), which store the neighbor information of visited nodes and the contents of visited vectors, respectively. When exploring a node _v_ in graph \(\mathcal{G}_\ell\), we first check whether \(v\in V_\ell^\mathcal{G}\). If so, the neighbor information of _v_ is retrieved from \(V_\ell^\mathcal{G}\), followed by a dummy graph access. Otherwise, _v_ and all its neighbor information are read from \(\mathcal{G}_\ell\) and stored in \(V_\ell^\mathcal{G}\) for future use. After obtaining the neighbor information, we access each neighbor’s vector to compute its query distance. Similarly, for each vector access, we first check \(V_\ell^\mathcal{D}\). If the vector is already present, it is retrieved from \(V_\ell^\mathcal{D}\), followed by a dummy vector access. Otherwise, it is loaded from \(\mathcal{D}_\ell\) and appended to \(V_\ell^\mathcal{D}\). Moreover, before processing multiple queries, we pre-shuffle both the graphs and the vector databases so that all nodes and vectors, including dummy ones, remain anonymous. More precisely, for each graph access, we first perform a linear scan of \(V_\ell^\mathcal{G}\). Then, depending on whether the target node is already in the cache, we access either the real node or a dummy node in the graph. Finally, we access \(V_\ell^\mathcal{G}\) again to store the newly retrieved real node or a dummy entry. Notably, we generate \(U\times T\) dummy nodes so that each graph access can use a different dummy node. Similarly, for each vector access, we first scan \(V_\ell^\mathcal{D}\), then access either a real or dummy vector, and finally store it in \(V_\ell^\mathcal{D}\).

## 6 BATCH QUERY PROOL IN PARALLEL

The preceding multiple-query protocol processes queries sequentially. We further consider the batch setting, where _U_ queries arrive together. We propose a batch protocol that processes the _U_ queries in parallel, reducing the round complexity from _O(U_) to _O_(log<sup>2</sup>_U_).

The key idea is to share vectors fetched by any query across all _U_ queries, so every query steps forward together by updating its own _C_ and _W_. Each iteration has two stages. First, the protocol obliviously deduplicates the nearest candidate from each query’s _C_, replaces duplicates with dummies, and issues _U_ distinct graph accesses. Second, it obliviously deduplicates the \(U\cdot M\) returned neighbor IDs and fetches \(U\cdot M\) vectors. Each query evaluates its distance to all \(U\cdot M\) fetched vectors, regardless of which query requested each vector. The batch therefore performs \(U^2\cdot M\) distance evaluations in parallel. These distances update the query’s own candidate set _C_ and result set _W_. The protocol records all fetched vectors in one global visited array _V_ shared by all queries. Each of the two oblivious deduplication steps sorts _O(U_) elements, requiring an oblivious sort network of depth _O_(log<sup>2</sup>_U_), which determines the per-iteration round cost. The full algorithm and the round-complexity proof appear in the extended version \[49\].

## 7 EVALUATION

In this section, we empirically evaluate HNSecW and aim to answer the following questions:

\(\bullet\) **Search quality.** What search quality does HNSecW achieve, and how does it perform when integrated into downstream RAG?

\(\bullet\) **Overhead.** What computation and communication overhead does HNSecW incur, and how does it perform against state-of-the- art secure ANN constructions?

### 7.1 Experimental Setup

**MPC Backends.** HNSecW can be instantiated with any semi- honest MPC protocol tolerating _t_ corruptions among _s_ servers. We evaluate two common configurations:

\(\bullet\) **Semi-honest 2PC (** _s=_2_,t=_1**).** Our 2PC uses ABY’s semi- honest mixed-protocol backend \[12\]. Arithmetic sharing handles distance computation. Boolean sharing handles visited checks. Yao’s garbled circuits handle comparisons, sorting, and candidate updates. ABY provides secure conversions among these representations.

## 8 RELATED WORK

**Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN).** ANN enables scalable similarity search in high-dimensional embedding spaces where exact _k_NN is often too expensive \[29, 30, 43\]. Classical methods include tree-based partitioning \[5\], locality-sensitive hashing \[22\], and vector quantization \[23\]. Graph-based indexes, such as HNSW \[32\] and NSG \[17\], dominate in practice, building proximity graphs for greedy query traversal. Recent systems extend graph-based ANN with improved indexing and retrieval strategies \[24, 42, 52\], while vector databases deploy these methods at scale \[10, 20, 40\].

**Secure ANN.** Prior work considers secure ANN under several threat models. When the database is public but the query is private, Tiptoe \[21\] searches a small candidate subset selected via clustering, trading accuracy for sublinear bandwidth and latency. Wally \[2\] further improves this pipeline’s throughput by batching queries, while Preco \[35\] reduces communication using two non-colluding servers. Pacmann \[50\] goes beyond clustering-based ANN methods by building a graph-index under query privacy. When both the database and query are private under a single owner (encrypted outsourcing), Compass \[51\] directly uses ORAM only to hide the server-side data access pattern, while executing the search logic in plaintext on the client. Instead, HERS \[15\] scans the encrypted database with FHE at high computational cost. SANNS \[11\] and PANTHER \[28\] use secure two-party computation between a server owning the database and a client owning the query. SANNS proposes a clustering-based secure ANN with optimized distance computation and top-_k_ selection, while PANTHER further improves end-to-end performance. In contrast, HNSecW secret-shares the query, database, and index among computation servers and achieves the same logarithmic complexity as the non-private setting. Notably, both SANNS \[11\] and PANTHER \[28\] can be adapted to secret-shared inputs. How ever, both approaches have \(O(\sqrt{N})\) complexity. Moreover, several early works \[34, 36, 38, 53\] studied secure _k_NN protocols, but they either target smaller-scale settings or apply only to the specialized secure settings discussed above.

## 9 CONCLUSION

We present HNSecW, an MPC ANN protocol with _O_(log_N_) online time and symmetric privacy for the query and database. It supports single-query, sequential multi-query, and batch-query settings. Future work includes more efficient secure index construction and dynamic graph updates. Currently, the database owner builds the index locally before queries arrive. For secure offloading, MPC servers can insert the _N_ vectors into the graph one by one and reuse our oblivious search to find neighbors. This requires _N_ graph searches, _O(N_log_N_) time, and _O(NM_) space for degree bound _M_ \[32\].
